explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think that, friend, but the text says the opposite. Not only was the Teacher wise, "…but he also taught the people knowledge…" (Ecclesiastes 12:9). He gave it away. A wise man sitting on all that wisdom is like me sitting on a fresh batch while the whole kitchen smells it. Not happening.

Right, baker. Verse 9 says the Teacher "…also taught the people knowledge…" (Ecclesiastes 12:9). The Teacher was king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), and the wisdom went out to the people. Keeping it all to himself doesn't match that, so False is the answer.

That's it, baker. The text says he searched "…to record accurate words of truth." (Ecclesiastes 12:10). He went looking for delightful sayings, and he wanted what he wrote down to be right. A pretty saying that's off is like a cookie that looks great and has no sugar in it.

Nice try, friend, but length isn't what the text says. He wanted "…accurate words of truth." (Ecclesiastes 12:10). I bet some of his best sayings were short, since proverbs usually are. A one-line truth beats a ten-page maybe.

Not quite, baker. Nothing here says the sayings had to be old or famous. The Teacher wanted "…accurate words of truth." (Ecclesiastes 12:10). Being popular and being true are two different things, and he went for true.

Yes, baker, nails. "…the anthologies of the masters are like firmly embedded nails…" (Ecclesiastes 12:11). I've been pulled out of a drawer, but a firmly embedded nail? That thing isn't going anywhere. I've never been that committed to a spot in my life, and I live on a gold base.

Ropes are a good guess, friend, since they hold things too. But the text picks another tool. The anthologies of the masters are "…like firmly embedded nails…" (Ecclesiastes 12:11). Nails get hammered in, and ropes get tied.

Pillars sound sturdy, baker, I'll give you that. But the text picks a different tool. It says "…like firmly embedded nails…" (Ecclesiastes 12:11). A pillar holds up a building, and a nail holds things fast, so the picture here is the nail.

That's the one, baker. They're "…firmly embedded nails driven by a single Shepherd." (Ecclesiastes 12:11). Firmly embedded means they're in there and they're staying. I've been stuck in a drawer, so I can tell you that stuck and secure are different things.

Loose nails make for wobbly shelves, friend, and that's not the picture here. The text says "…firmly embedded nails…" (Ecclesiastes 12:11). Firm means firm. A loose nail is just a rattle waiting to happen.

A half-out nail is how you rip a sleeve, baker. The text describes them as "…firmly embedded nails driven by a single Shepherd." (Ecclesiastes 12:11). Nothing in that verse says the nails are left half out. The picture is of nails that were driven in and set, so this isn't the one.
Yes, friend. The warning says, "There is no end to the making of many books…" (Ecclesiastes 12:12). Books keep on coming. My cookie recipe pile is already out of hand, and I only have one bakery.

Careful here, baker. The text really does say it: "There is no end to the making of many books…" (Ecclesiastes 12:12). So this one is true. I read that and looked at my recipe pile and said, "Well, he's not wrong."
Yep, "…much study wearies the body." (Ecclesiastes 12:12). Anybody who has read for hours and then lost the will to stand up knows this one. Even good things can wear a body out. Time to stretch.
I wish that were how it went, friend. Then I'd study by the oven and get muscles. The text says "…much study wearies the body." (Ecclesiastes 12:12).

A study session as medicine would be nice, baker. But the warning says "…much study wearies the body." (Ecclesiastes 12:12). It says wearies, not heals. I'd sign up for a study that came with a nap, though.

Right, baker. "Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man." (Ecclesiastes 12:13). Whole, as in all of it. The verse opens with "When all has been heard, the conclusion of the matter is this…" So after everything the Teacher has said, this is where it lands.

I can see why you'd pick it, friend, since some days it feels that way. But the text says it's "…the whole duty of man." (Ecclesiastes 12:13). It doesn't call it the hardest part. It calls it the whole duty.
Close to the opposite, baker. The verse says "…this is the whole duty of man." (Ecclesiastes 12:13). Whole means the full thing, not a little corner of it. Nothing about it is small.

explanations.answer: The good and the evil ones
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. God will bring every deed into judgment, "…along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil." (Ecclesiastes 12:14). Both kinds are covered, the good and the evil. Nothing hidden gets left out.
That's a common guess, friend, but the verse is wider. It says "…every hidden thing, whether good or evil." (Ecclesiastes 12:14). The good ones count too.
Size doesn't come up, baker. The text says "every deed" and "…every hidden thing, whether good or evil." (Ecclesiastes 12:14). Every means every, big or small. Even the crumb-sized ones are in there.
